o: A subsequence with indices i₀<i₁<… is balanced when nums[iⱼ] − nums[iⱼ₋₁] ≥ iⱼ − iⱼ₋₁, i.e., nums[i] − i is non-decreasing along the subsequence. So after transforming b[i] = nums[i] − i, we need the maximum-sum non-decreasing subsequence. Negative answers are possible (example 3 returns −1), so we can't assume the empty subsequence.
k: Substitute b[i] = nums[i] − i: balance becomes 'b non-decreasing along the subsequence'.
This is maximum-sum non-decreasing subsequence: dp[i] = nums[i] + max{dp[j] : j < i, b[j] ≤ b[i]}, solved with a Fenwick tree for prefix-maximum over compressed b values.
The answer is the max over all i of dp[i] (each single element is a valid subsequence).

a.i: Compress b values. Process indices left to right; a Fenwick tree indexed by compressed b stores the best dp achieved with b-value ≤ query point. dp[i] = nums[i] + prefixMax(b[i]); then insert dp[i] at b[i]. Querying before inserting enforces j < i automatically.
s: Compute b[i] = nums[i] − i and coordinate-compress.
For each i in order: dp = nums[i] + query(rank(b[i])); update tree at rank(b[i]) with dp; track global max.
a.t: O(n log n) — compression plus one Fenwick operation per element

a.n: Approach 2: Segment Tree (Same Idea, Different Structure)
a.i: Identical DP but with a segment tree over compressed b-values supporting range-max queries on [0, rank(b[i])]. Useful if you later need range updates beyond prefix maxima; otherwise Fenwick is simpler.
s: Build a max segment tree initialized to −∞.
For each i, query max over ranks ≤ rank(b[i]), form dp, point-update rank(b[i]).
a.t: O(n log n) — same asymptotics as Fenwick, larger constants

w: The crux is spotting the b[i] = nums[i] − i transformation; afterwards it's a textbook weighted LIS variant. Pitfall: all-negative arrays — clamp prev contributions at 0 and initialize the answer to −∞, not 0. Follow-up: report the actual subsequence (store parent pointers alongside dp).
